analysis.one_liner: Doubles the tax credits and pre-tax accounts families use to pay for child care.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved before the 118th Congress ended, so the doubled child care tax benefits never took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would double three tax provisions tied to child care: the cap on the child and dependent care credit (from $3,000 to $6,000 for one child and from $6,000 to $12,000 for two or more), the amount workers can set aside pre-tax in a dependent care assistance account (from $5,000 to $10,000), and the maximum tax credit an employer can claim for providing or supporting child care (from $150,000 to $300,000). It applies to tax years starting after December 31, 2023, and includes no offsetting revenue. [S3] [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Working families who pay for child care out of pocket would be able to claim credit for a larger share of those expenses. Workers whose employers offer dependent care accounts could shelter twice as much of their pay from taxes for child care costs. Employers that build or operate on-site child care could claim a much larger credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working parents paying for child care

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the expense caps for the child and dependent care credit, from $3,000 to $6,000 for one qualifying person and from $6,000 to $12,000 for two or more, letting families wipe more of their child care spending off their tax bill. [S3]
Doubles the annual limit on dependent care assistance programs (pre-tax accounts many employers offer) from $5,000 to $10,000, so workers can pay for twice as much care with untaxed earnings. [S3]
Doubles the cap on the employer-provided child care credit from $150,000 to $300,000, giving businesses a bigger tax credit for building or running child care for their employees. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury picks up the full cost, since the bill contains no offsetting revenue or tax increase, and general taxpayers ultimately bear that. Because the child and dependent care credit is a non-refundable credit, the lowest-income families — who owe little or no federal income tax — get little or nothing from the doubled credit, while families with real tax bills benefit most.

drawbacks.text: The child and dependent care credit is non-refundable, so it only offsets taxes a family actually owes; families with the lowest incomes, who often need child care help most, would see little or no benefit from the doubled credit. [S3]
The bill raises no revenue to pay for the roughly doubled limits; the added cost would go to the federal deficit unless Congress offsets it elsewhere. [S3]
The dependent care account expansion only helps workers whose employers offer such accounts, which skews the benefit toward workers at larger employers. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For middle-income families juggling child care costs, doubling the credit and account limits is real, immediate relief — child care often runs thousands of dollars a year per child. The honest tradeoffs are that the design leaves out the lowest-income families (a non-refundable credit helps only those who owe tax), and the cost is added to the deficit with no pay-for. The employer credit doubling is the weakest piece for the public: it is a business tax break whose benefit to families depends entirely on employers choosing to build child care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 5, 2024 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it died without a vote. [S5] [S1]

narrative.text: Rep. Marcus Molinaro (R-NY) introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, joined by Rep. Sharice Davids (D-KS), and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S5] [S3]
No further action was ever recorded: the Ways and Means Committee held no markup and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the federal Treasury keeps the money the doubled benefits would have cost. Working families paying for child care got no relief, and the child care cost squeeze they faced is untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; child care families gained nothing

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 5, 2024 and never took up the bill; no markup, no vote, no report before the Congress ended. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill with two Democratic cosponsors and no recorded opposition from any member; the bill died from committee inaction rather than a party split. [S3] [S4] [S5]

industries.note: Doubling the family credit and pre-tax account limits would put more purchasing power in parents' hands for child care, and a bigger employer credit would push more businesses to fund care. Providers would see more customers and investment; families get help affording care. [S3]
The employer-provided child care credit cap would double from $150,000 to $300,000 per year, a larger tax break for businesses that provide or support child care for workers. [S3]
